# Corruption scandal: Durban businessman and high ranking cops granted bail

## Court

![](https://iol-prod.appspot.com/image/cec45dd96fcc88e78b943edd3618ca7835dde798=w700)

Durban businessman Tariq Downes, Crime Intelligence head Major-General Feroz Khan and Gauteng Hawks head Major General Ebrahim Kadwa.

Image: Itumeleng English/ Independent Newspapers

DURBAN businessman Tariq Downes, Crime Intelligence head Major-General Feroz Khan and Gauteng Hawks head Major General Ebrahim Kadwa, have been granted bail following their arrests for their alleged involvement in a corruption scandal linked to illicit precious metals.

The men appeared in the Kempton Park Magistrate’s Court on Monday, where they were each released on R20 000 bail, IOL reported.

The matter has adjourned to June 14. 

Police said their arrests followed an investigation into alleged illicit precious metals transactions, corruption and related offences.

“The arrests were effected over the weekend by the team who executed a J50 warrant of arrest,” police said in a statement.

Kadwa was arrested on Saturday, while Khan was taken into custody on Sunday after law enforcement officers raided his apartment in Houghton, Johannesburg.

The arrests placed renewed attention on long-standing allegations against Khan, who has previously been accused of political interference and corruption.

During testimony before the Madlanga Commission and Parliament’s Ad Hoc Committee, KZN Police Commissioner Lt-Gen. Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi described Khan as a “political fixer” who allegedly received protection from senior politicians.

Mkhwanazi also claimed former police minister Bheki Cele pressured him in 2021 to shield Khan during investigations linked to a major drug bust.

Khan was previously accused of defeating the ends of justice and bringing the SAPS into disrepute after allegedly interfering in the investigation when officers reportedly attempted to steal seized narcotics.

# Corruption-accused Durban businessman maintains his innocence

Monday 11 May 2026 - 15:00pm

![Durban businessman, Tariq Downes insists that he is innocent and that there is no case against him. ](/sites/default/files/styles/banner_image/public/2026-05/Screenshot%202026-05-11%20140923.png.webp?itok=OqnihbPQ)

[](https://www.addtoany.com/share#url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.enca.com%2Fnews-top-stories%2Fcorruption-accused-durban-businessman-maintains-his-innocence&title=Corruption-accused%20Durban%20businessman%20maintains%20his%20innocence)

JOHANNESBURG - Durban businessman, Tariq Downes, insists that he is innocent and that there is no case against him. 

Downes appeared at the Kempton Park Magistrate’s Court on Monday alongside two SAPS major-generals, Feroz Khan and Ebrahim Kadwa. 

The three were arrested over the weekend after they were allegedly linked to the illegal dealing and unlawful possession of precious metals following an intensive investigation by the Gauteng Counter Intelligence Operations (GCI-OPS).

**READ |** [**Senior cop Feroz Khan expected in court after weekend arrest**](https://www.enca.com/news-top-stories-videos/senior-cop-feroz-khan-expected-court-after-weekend-arrest)

They face charges including the unlawful dealing in precious metals, defeating the ends of justice, corruption and contravention of applicable legislation regulating precious metals in South Africa.

The trio was granted R20,000 bail under the conditions that they do not interfere with the investigations, or, contact witnesses. 

They are also required to hand in their passports to the investigative officer on or before 12 May. 

Their case has been postponed to 14 July for further investigations.

BUSINESSMAN AND TWO SENIOR POLICE OFFICIALS APPEAR IN COURT ON PRECIOUS METALS AND DEFEATING THE ENDS OF JUSTICE CHARGES

Businessman Tariq Downes, the Head of Counter-Intelligence in the South African Police Service (SAPS) Crime Intelligence division Major-General Feroz Khan, and the Gauteng Provincial Head of the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation (DPCI), Major-General Ebrahim Ahmed Kadwa, made their first appearance before the Kempton Park Magistrates’ Court on charges of contravening the Precious Metals Act and defeating or obstructing the course of justice.

The charges emanate from an incident on 05 May 2021, when Downes was allegedly found in possession of 75.9 grams of unwrought gold, valued at approximately R62 836, at OR Tambo International Airport. During questioning, he allegedly claimed the metal was a brass bar and that he was acting as an undercover agent linked to senior SAPS officials. Investigations allegedly established that no authorised undercover operation involving precious metals existed at the time. The state further alleges that Khan and Kadwa instructed officers to release Downes despite there being no supporting documentation for such an operation.

The case was postponed to 14 July 2026 for further investigation. The three were each granted bail of R20 000 with conditions. The NPA remains committed to ensuring accountability and upholding the rule of law, regardless of the status or seniority of those implicated in criminal conduct.

A major corruption case is shaking South Africa’s law enforcement leadership after a Durban businessman and two senior police generals appeared in court linked to alleged illegal precious metals dealings.

According to reports, Durban businessman Tariq Downes, along with Crime Intelligence head Major-General Feroz Khan and Gauteng Hawks head Major-General Ebrahim Kadwa, have all been granted bail after their arrests in a widening corruption investigation.

Here’s what has been confirmed so far:

• The trio appeared at the Kempton Park Magistrate’s Court

• Each was released on R20,000 bail

• The case has been postponed to 14 June

• Arrests were carried out over the weekend following a J50 warrant operation

• The investigation relates to alleged illicit precious metals transactions, corruption, and related offences

• Khan was reportedly arrested after a raid at his apartment in Houghton, Johannesburg

Police say the operation is part of a deeper probe into organised corruption networks involving high-ranking officials and business figures.

The case has also revived controversy around Major-General Feroz Khan, who has previously faced allegations of political interference and misconduct. Testimony from earlier commissions has linked him to claims of protection from senior political figures and interference in sensitive investigations.

With senior police leadership now under scrutiny, this case is expected to intensify public debate about corruption within South Africa’s law enforcement structures.

There is a strange but powerful image of a man handing a bag of blood to a mosquito, as if offering a bribe to something that already survives on what is being offered. The absurdity is the point: the mosquito responds, “Sorry, I don’t accept bribes,” which immediately turns the story into a reflection on human society rather than nature. In South Africa, bribery is often not seen in dramatic forms but in everyday moments—at traffic stops, licensing offices, municipal queues, and informal negotiations where people try to “speed things up” with money or favours. Yet what begins as convenience slowly becomes corruption, and what begins as survival logic can harden into a system where fairness is no longer the standard, but negotiation is. As Scripture warns, “You shall not pervert justice… you shall not accept a bribe” (Deuteronomy 16:19), reminding us that justice is meant to be consistent, not flexible to influence. The deeper issue is that bribery does not only change outcomes, it changes thinking—people begin to believe that nothing moves without payment, and that belief becomes more damaging than the act itself. Even humour exposes the truth: one could imagine a driver at a roadblock trying to “negotiate” with a mosquito-like officer, only to be met with silence and refusal, highlighting how ridiculous corruption becomes when stripped of its excuses. The philosopher Aristotle once said, “We are what we repeatedly do,” and in that sense, repeated small corruptions slowly reshape an entire society’s moral expectations. There is also a kind of poetic truth in the contrast: a mosquito, driven only by instinct, does not accept or reject bribes, yet humans—who possess conscience, law, and choice—often struggle with what even nature does not require. In that tension lies the warning: when corruption becomes normal, it no longer feels like wrongdoing but like routine navigation of life. And perhaps that is why the image lingers—because it quietly asks whether it is the system that is broken, or the choices within it that have stopped resisting.

In the same reflection, imagine a man like Ferrell Govender inside the prison system, where the lines between authority, survival, and desperation blur in uncomfortable ways. In that environment, stories circulate of prisoners trying to “soften” conditions by slipping money or favours to guards—paying for extra comfort, faster movement, or quieter treatment—turning correctional spaces into shadow economies where rules bend under pressure. Whether real or fictional in its telling, the symbolism remains powerful: when even confinement becomes negotiable through bribery, the idea of justice begins to weaken at its core. It ties back to the earlier image of the mosquito refusing a bag of blood—because in contrast, human systems often do accept what nature would ignore. As Scripture reminds us, “a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise” (Deuteronomy 16:19), suggesting that corruption does not only change actions, but distorts perception itself. In South Africa’s broader reality, this becomes a mirror of how informal payments can creep into even the most controlled environments, from streets to institutions designed for discipline. The humour in imagining a mosquito refusing payment while humans negotiate morality only deepens the irony: we are the only beings who must choose between principle and convenience, yet often struggle to choose principle. In that sense, the prison wall, like the street corner or the government office, becomes another stage where the same question is asked in different forms—what is justice worth when it is constantly being offered a price?

Gauteng Hawks head Ebrahim Kadwa, Crime Intelligence senior cop Feroz Khan and Durban businessman Tariq Downes appear before the Kempton Park Magistrates Court on 11 May 2026. Picture: Sphamandla Dlamini/EWN

A businessman arrested alongside two senior police officers for allegedly dealing in illicit gold said he believes the case against him is baseless.

Businessman Tariq Downes appeared in the Kempton Park Magistrates Court on Monday, alongside Gauteng Hawks head Ebrahim Kadwa and Counter-Intelligence head Feroz Khan.

They were all arrested by the Political Killings Task Team (PKTT) over the weekend.

It is alleged that Downes was found in possession of a gold bar at OR Tambo International Airport in 2021 and contacted Kadwa and Khan in an attempt to have the case buried.

The State claims that Downes was found in possession of unwrought gold in May 2021 and told the cops he was an undercover police agent.

However, the officers who arrested him didn’t buy his story and refused to release him from custody.

Khan and Kadwa were then contacted to verify whether Downes was a police agent, to which the pair allegedly confirmed and ordered his release.

Police investigations later allegedly revealed that this was a lie and that Downes had never been a member of the police service.

After being released on bail, this is what the businessman said to journalists: “There is no case against me. They sent the Political Killings Task Team for me, but I have never even voted in my life.”

They were released on bail and will return to court on 14 July.
